title: Why the platypus puzzled scientists: George Shaw's 1799 specimen and the animal's unusual features

sources.title: Chapter 7. The platypus frontier: eggs, Aborigines and empire in 19th century Queensland (Libby Robin)
Australian Dictionary of Biography: George Shaw
David Attenborough - the platypus (The Science Show)

facts.text: George Shaw, a keeper at the British Museum, described the platypus scientifically in 1799.
The skin Shaw examined had been sent from New South Wales.
Some people suspected a hoax, such as a duck's bill attached to the body of a mole.
At first Shaw wondered whether someone had stitched parts of different animals together as a joke.
Shaw cut the skin with scissors to check whether the bill had been stitched on; the scissor marks can still be seen on the skin.
The bill turned out to be attached naturally to the furry skin of the head.
The platypus has fur, webbed feet, a broad tail and a duck-like bill.
Females lay two soft-shelled eggs and keep them against the belly with the tail.
Platypuses have no teats; milk seeps onto patches of skin and the young feed from them.
When diving, a platypus keeps its eyes, ears and nostrils shut.
The bill detects electrical signals in the water, which helps the platypus find prey with its eyes closed.
When prey such as a shrimp moves, its muscle contraction makes a small electrical signal that the bill can pick up.
It eats small water animals such as insect larvae, freshwater shrimp and crayfish.
Males have spurs on their ankles that are linked to venom glands.
The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs and feeds its young milk.
